subsection: 2. Case study: the 1848 Revolution in Germany

notes.h: 1848 across Europe: the year of revolutions
notes.b: In 1848 revolutions broke out in one capital after another within a few weeks. Germany was one part of a Europe-wide wave, so it helps to know the pattern before looking at the German case.
points: The first rising came in Palermo in January 1848. Then Paris rose on 22-24 February, when King Louis-Philippe fell and the Second Republic was declared; this news was the spark for the rest.

The risings then came fast: Vienna on 13 March, Budapest on 15 March, Venice on 17 March, and Berlin and Milan on 18 March (Milan's Five Days of street fighting ran 18-22 March). Prague's rising came later, in June.

The common causes were the crop failures and economic depression of 1846-47, which made ordinary people desperate, and middle-class liberal demands for constitutions (written limits on a ruler's power).

Nationalism (the wish of a people with a shared language and culture to form its own state) drove Germans, Italians, Hungarians and Czechs alike, so each rising had a national as well as a liberal side.
The example of Paris spread so quickly because newspapers, railways and the telegraph carried the news within days, which encouraged crowds elsewhere to press their own rulers.
Britain and Russia escaped revolution in 1848. By 1849 nearly every rising had been defeated by the old monarchies and their armies, a pattern the German case follows.
notes.tip: For a 'year of revolutions' question, give the common causes and the speed of the spread, then use Germany as your main example with brief comparison to Paris and Vienna.

notes.h: Starting point: the German Confederation before 1848
notes.b: To understand 1848 in Germany you need to know what the revolutionaries wanted to change. Germany was not one country but a loose league of states.
points: The German Confederation, set up in 1815, was a loose league of German states (39 at its foundation) with a Diet, its assembly of state delegates, at Frankfurt under Austrian presidency. Austria and Prussia were the two great powers inside it.

Metternich's system of repression, meaning censorship, police spies and the Carlsbad Decrees of 1819, had kept liberal and national movements down. His fall in March 1848 removed the system's chief defender.
The Zollverein (customs union) of 1834 had already linked most German states economically under Prussia, with Austria outside it, so many Germans were used to thinking of a Germany without Austria.

notes.b: The German revolution grew out of economic distress, liberal frustration with the system of 1815 and the wish for a united German nation. Each cause affected a different group, and news from Paris in February 1848 acted as the trigger.
points: Potato blight from 1845 and poor grain harvests in 1846 and 1847 sharply raised food prices, so the poor went hungry and hunger riots broke out in many areas.

A commercial and industrial depression in 1847 brought bankruptcies and unemployment. It hit artisans (skilled craftsmen) already threatened by factory competition; the Silesian weavers' rising of 1844 had shown the desperation of hand workers.
Liberals, mostly educated middle-class men, wanted constitutions, freedom of the press and assembly, trial by jury and a German national parliament.
Nationalists wanted a German nation state, but disagreed whether it should include the German lands of the Habsburg Empire, the territories ruled by Austria's emperor.
Peasants in the south and west wanted an end to the remaining feudal dues and services owed to landlords, which were a burden left over from the old order.
Liberal opposition had grown in the southern state parliaments and in Prussia's United Diet of 1847, which refused to vote a loan for a railway without constitutional concessions from the king.
The trigger was the news of the February revolution in Paris, which showed that a monarch could be overthrown and encouraged all these groups to act at once.
notes.tip: Higher essays reward a separate paragraph on economic, liberal, national and trigger causes, each tied to a specific event: hunger and depression of 1846-47, the United Diet of 1847 and the Paris news.

notes.b: Within weeks of the Paris revolution, rulers across the German states gave way to crowds rather than risk being overthrown. The pattern was protest, then concession.
points: A mass meeting at Mannheim in Baden on 27 February 1848 demanded a free press, trial by jury, citizens' militias and a German parliament, and these March demands spread across the states.
Rulers appointed liberal March ministries, promised constitutions and lifted censorship in Baden, Württemberg, Hesse, Saxony and Hanover, because they feared a revolution like the one in Paris.
In Bavaria, Ludwig I, already discredited by his affair with the dancer Lola Montez, abdicated in March 1848.
In Berlin, troops fired on a crowd on 18 March, and a night of barricade fighting left about 200 to 300 civilians dead (sources differ).
On 19 March Frederick William IV withdrew the troops from Berlin and was forced to bare his head before the bodies of the dead in the palace courtyard, a public sign of surrender.
On 21 March he rode through Berlin wearing the black, red and gold colours of German nationalism and declared that Prussia would merge into Germany.

He appointed a liberal ministry under the Rhineland businessmen Camphausen and Hansemann and called a Prussian National Assembly, elected in May 1848. Do not confuse it with the all-German assembly at Frankfurt.
Peasant risings in the south-west in March forced governments to begin abolishing feudal dues.
notes.tip: For Ordinary Level, learn the concessions in the states and the Berlin sequence of 18, 19 and 21 March. Use the range for Berlin's dead, not a single figure.

notes.h: The Vorparlament and the first republican rising
notes.b: The liberals who now held influence needed a way to create a German parliament. They began with an informal meeting, which also showed the split between moderates and radicals.
points: The Vorparlament (pre-parliament), a self-appointed gathering of liberal politicians, met at Frankfurt from 31 March to 3 April 1848. It was not the Frankfurt National Assembly, which came later.

It rejected the radicals' call for a republic and arranged elections to a national assembly by broad manhood suffrage (the vote for adult men), although each state set its own rules and some excluded servants and men on poor relief.
Disappointed radicals in Baden, led by Friedrich Hecker and Gustav Struve, launched a republican rising in April 1848, which federal troops defeated at Kandern on 20 April.

notes.b: The elected assembly met in May 1848 and was meant to write a constitution for all Germany. Its membership explains both its quality and its weakness.
points: The Frankfurt National Assembly opened on 18 May 1848 in the Paulskirche (St Paul's Church) in Frankfurt.

About 800 men sat at some point, including substitutes, because membership changed over time. Most were lawyers, judges, civil servants, teachers and professors, so it was nicknamed the professors' parliament.
Craftsmen were few, and there were almost no peasants or workers among the deputies, which means the poor were barely represented and had little reason to defend the Assembly.
The Assembly elected Heinrich von Gagern, a moderate liberal from Hesse-Darmstadt, as its president, which shows that moderates led it.
Deputies formed clubs named after their meeting places, the forerunners of German political parties, broadly a right, a liberal centre and a democratic left.

On 29 June 1848 it chose Archduke John of Austria as Reichsverweser (imperial regent) at the head of a Provisional Central Power. This government had no army, civil service or tax revenue of its own, so it relied on the state governments.
notes.tip: Examiners link the Assembly's make-up to its failure: a body of educated men with no army or administration. Keep the Frankfurt Assembly separate from the Prussian National Assembly in Berlin.

notes.h: The Assembly's work: Basic Rights and the national question
notes.b: The Assembly had to decide what rights Germans should have and which territory the new Germany should cover. The first was settled, but the second divided it.
points: The Basic Rights of the German People, passed in December 1848, guaranteed equality before the law, freedom of the press, speech, religion, assembly and movement, and trial by jury.
They abolished the nobility as a privileged estate, landlords' private courts and feudal dues, and abolished the death penalty except under martial law.
Grossdeutsch (Greater German) meant a Germany including the German-speaking Habsburg lands. Catholics, Austrians and many southerners favoured it.
Kleindeutsch (Lesser German) meant a Germany united under Prussia without Austria. Gagern and most Protestant northern liberals favoured it.

The Grossdeutsch plan failed because Prince Felix Schwarzenberg, Austria's chief minister from November 1848, insisted, finally in March 1849, that the whole multinational Habsburg Empire must enter any German state or none of it would.

The Assembly also voted in 1848 to include part of the Prussian province of Posen, where Poles were the majority, and Czech leaders refused to send deputies to Frankfurt. Liberal nationalism could deny other nations' rights.
notes.tip: Students often swap the two terms: Grossdeutsch means with Austria, Kleindeutsch means without it. Do not credit the Basic Rights to the king of Prussia.

notes.b: A quarrel over two border duchies tested the Assembly's power and exposed that it could not enforce its will.
points: The duchies of Schleswig and Holstein were ruled by the King of Denmark. Holstein, wholly German, belonged to the German Confederation, while Schleswig, with a mixed Danish and German population, did not.
When the new Danish king, Frederick VII, moved to incorporate Schleswig into Denmark in March 1848, the German population rose and set up a provisional government at Kiel.
Prussian troops under General Wrangel invaded on the Confederation's behalf, which the Assembly hailed as a national war.
Under pressure from Britain and Russia, Prussia signed the Malmö armistice in August 1848 without consulting Frankfurt.
The Assembly first rejected the armistice and then, having no army of its own, accepted it on 16 September 1848, which showed its dependence on Prussia.

Radicals rioted in Frankfurt on 18 September and murdered two conservative deputies, Prince Felix Lichnowsky and General Hans von Auerswald. The Assembly had to be saved by Prussian and Austrian troops.
Fighting resumed in 1849, but Prussia made peace with Denmark in 1850, the duchies' army was defeated at Idstedt in July 1850, and the London Protocol of 1852 confirmed the Danish king's rule.
notes.tip: Use Malmö and the September riots as the supporting events when you argue the Assembly was powerless. Do not confuse Prince Felix Schwarzenberg with Prince Felix Lichnowsky.

notes.h: The recovery of Austria and Prussia, late 1848
notes.b: By late 1848 the old governments had regained control of their capitals through force, while the liberals at Frankfurt were still debating.
points: In June 1848 the Austrian general Windischgrätz bombarded Prague and crushed the Czech rising, and in July Radetzky defeated Piedmont at Custoza.
A radical rising in Vienna in October 1848 was crushed when Windischgrätz and the Croatian commander Jelačić retook the city on 31 October.

Robert Blum, a radical Frankfurt deputy from Saxony, was shot in Vienna on 9 November 1848, despite his immunity as a member of the Assembly, which showed how little the Assembly's protection was worth.
Schwarzenberg became Austrian chief minister in November, and on 2 December 1848 the 18-year-old Franz Joseph replaced Emperor Ferdinand.
In Berlin, Frederick William IV appointed a conservative ministry under Count Brandenburg, and General Wrangel's troops entered the city on 10 November 1848 without resistance.
On 5 December 1848 the king dissolved the Prussian National Assembly and imposed a constitution of his own, which kept royal control of the army and ministers.

In May 1849 Prussia brought in the three-class franchise, which divided voters into three classes by the taxes they paid. Each class chose a third of the electors, so a small wealthy minority had a vastly greater say than the poor majority.
notes.tip: Use Prague, Vienna and Berlin retaken as your evidence that the rulers kept loyal armies. Do not mix up Schwarzenberg (minister), Windischgrätz and Radetzky (generals) and Jelačić (Croatian commander).

notes.h: The imperial constitution and the refused crown, 1849
notes.b: With Austria and Prussia recovering, the Assembly finished its constitution and offered the crown to Prussia's king. His answer decided the revolution's fate.
points: The Frankfurt constitution, completed on 27-28 March 1849, created a federal German Empire with a hereditary emperor, a lower house elected by manhood suffrage and an upper house representing the states.
On 28 March 1849 the Assembly elected Frederick William IV Emperor of the Germans by 290 votes, with 248 deputies abstaining.

Frederick William gave an evasive answer to the Assembly's delegation on 3 April and formally refused the crown on 28 April 1849. He would not accept a crown from an elected assembly rather than from his fellow princes, and he feared Austria's reaction.
In private he described it as a crown from the gutter, tainted by revolution.
Austria rejected the constitution and recalled its deputies in April 1849, because a German empire without Austria threatened its position.
Twenty-eight smaller states accepted the constitution by mid-April, but Prussia, Bavaria, Saxony and Hanover rejected it, so it never came into force.
notes.tip: The formal refusal was on 28 April 1849, not 3 April. For Ordinary Level, his refusal is the standard example of the revolutionaries' failure.

notes.h: The final phase: the rump parliament and the 1849 risings
notes.b: After the crown was refused, radicals tried to force the princes to accept the constitution, and Prussian troops put them down.
points: In May 1849 radicals rose in Saxony, the Palatinate and Baden to force the princes to accept the constitution. Richard Wagner and Mikhail Bakunin took part in the Dresden rising.

Prussian troops crushed the Dresden rising in May and the Baden and Palatinate risings by July 1849, when the fortress of Rastatt surrendered. The Baden campaign was commanded by Prince William of Prussia, the later William I.
Some rebels were executed and many imprisoned, and thousands fled, so the radical movement lost many of its leaders.
The moderates left Frankfurt, and about 100 radical deputies moved to Stuttgart as a rump parliament (a small remnant of the Assembly) until Württemberg troops dispersed them on 18 June 1849.
Thousands of revolutionaries emigrated, many to the United States, where these Forty-Eighters included Friedrich Hecker and Carl Schurz.

notes.h: Prussia's Erfurt Union and the humiliation of Olmütz
notes.b: Prussia then tried to gain the unity the Assembly had failed to win, but Austria was strong enough to stop it.
points: The Erfurt Union plan, drawn up by Joseph von Radowitz in 1849-50, aimed at a Kleindeutsch union under Prussia by agreement of the princes, and an Erfurt Parliament met in March-April 1850. It is not the Zollverein of 1834.
Austria, backed by Russia, threatened war, and by the Punctation of Olmütz (29 November 1850) Prussia abandoned the union. Prussians remembered it as the humiliation of Olmütz, a defeat for Prussia.
The old Confederation and its Diet were restored in 1851 under Austrian presidency, and the Diet repealed the Basic Rights that year.
Otto von Bismarck was Prussia's delegate at the Diet in Frankfurt from 1851, so he saw Austrian power at close quarters.
notes.tip: Olmütz was a defeat for Prussia, not for Austria. It makes a good closing point in a failure essay, since Prussia later reversed it under Bismarck.

notes.b: The revolution failed for several linked reasons. The strongest answers weigh them: the Assembly lacked force while the rulers kept theirs, and the other causes follow from that.
points: The Frankfurt Assembly had no army, money or administration, so it depended on the very governments it was trying to limit. The Malmö armistice and the September riots showed this.
The rulers kept control of their armies and bureaucracies, which stayed loyal and were used to retake Prague, Vienna and Berlin once the shock of March had passed.
Liberals were divided from radicals and workers: middle-class deputies feared a social revolution and a republic more than they feared the princes.
Peasants lost interest once governments abolished most feudal dues in 1848, as Austria did in September 1848, so they stopped supporting the revolution.
Months of debate on the Basic Rights and the Grossdeutsch-Kleindeutsch question gave Austria and Prussia time to recover.
National rivalries with Danes, Poles and Czechs split the revolutionaries and gave the Habsburg army willing allies, such as Jelačić's Croats.
Austria recovered and Russia backed the old order; Russia also crushed Hungary in 1849.
The refusal of the crown by Frederick William IV left the constitution without the one state strong enough to enforce it.
notes.tip: Rank the reasons rather than listing them, and give each an event: Malmö and the September riots for powerlessness, Prague, Vienna and Berlin for loyal armies, the refused crown for dependence on Prussia. For Ordinary Level, learn the reasons above.

notes.h: Assessment: results, significance and differing views
notes.b: Judging 1848 means weighing what it achieved against what it failed to do, and comparing how people saw it then and later.
points: Failure: no united Germany was created, the Basic Rights were repealed by the restored Diet in 1851, and the old Confederation returned.
Achievement: feudal dues and serfdom were abolished, so peasants gained a lasting benefit, and Prussia kept a constitution and parliament after 1850, however limited.

Failure: liberals were discredited as impractical, and many concluded that unity would come only through Prussian power, not speeches and majority votes, a lesson Bismarck confirmed in his 'blood and iron' speech of 1862.
Achievement: the Assembly was Germany's first national parliament, created political parties and provided a model for the Weimar constitution of 1919 and the Basic Law of 1949.

Contemporary views: conservatives celebrated the restoration of order, while radicals and exiles, including Marx and Engels, blamed the cowardice of the liberal middle class. Marx edited the Neue Rheinische Zeitung in Cologne in 1848-49.
Later views: A. J. P. Taylor wrote in 1945 that 'German history reached its turning-point and failed to turn', linked to the Sonderweg idea of a German special path away from liberal democracy.
More recent historians stress the revolution's lasting gains in political culture and participation.
notes.tip: Give achievements and failures as paired points, then a verdict. For documents questions, the answer that earns marks is generally no, because the old rulers regained control by 1849, with one supporting fact. Use a historian's view to support a judgement.

keyTerms.definition: In 1848, the demand of the educated middle class for a constitution, an elected parliament, civil liberties and the rule of law.
In 1848, the demand that all Germans be united in a single nation state with a national parliament instead of the 39 states of the Confederation.
Government by the people through elected representatives chosen by all adult men, demanded by the radicals of 1848, who also wanted a republic.
The self-appointed pre-parliament that met at Frankfurt from 31 March to 3 April 1848 and arranged elections to a national assembly.
The elected German parliament that met in the Paulskirche from 18 May 1848 to draw up a constitution for a united Germany.
The civil liberties declared by the Frankfurt Assembly in December 1848, including equality before the law, a free press and the end of feudal privileges.
The Greater German solution: a united Germany that would include the German-speaking lands of the Habsburg Empire.
The Lesser German solution: a united Germany under Prussian leadership that excluded Austria.
Imperial regent: the title given by the Frankfurt Assembly in June 1848 to Archduke John of Austria as head of a provisional German government.
The August 1848 truce between Prussia and Denmark over Schleswig-Holstein, which the Assembly was forced to accept, exposing its weakness.
The Prussian voting system of 1849 that divided voters into three classes by taxes paid, giving the wealthy most of the voting power.
The November 1850 agreement by which Prussia, under Austrian and Russian pressure, abandoned the Erfurt Union and accepted the restored Confederation.

factCards.definition: Crop failures and hunger (1845–47), the 1847 depression, liberal and nationalist demands, and the example of the February revolution in Paris.
Barricade fighting left about 300 dead; Frederick William IV withdrew the troops, honoured the dead and rode through Berlin in the German colours.
It opened on 18 May 1848 in the Paulskirche; about 585 deputies were elected, mostly lawyers, officials and academics.
Friedrich Hecker and Gustav Struve led a republican rising in Baden that federal troops defeated at Kandern on 20 April 1848.
Prussia fought Denmark for the duchies but signed the Malmö armistice in August; the Assembly's acceptance led to the Frankfurt riots of 18 September.
Windischgrätz took Prague in June and Vienna on 31 October; Robert Blum was shot on 9 November and Franz Joseph became emperor on 2 December.
Wrangel's troops entered Berlin on 10 November, and on 5 December the king dissolved the Prussian Assembly and imposed his own constitution.
The Assembly elected Frederick William IV Emperor of the Germans by 290 votes with 248 abstentions; he refused the crown on 28 April.
Risings in Saxony, the Palatinate and Baden in support of the constitution were crushed by Prussian troops by July 1849.

factCards.term: End of the rump parliament, June 1849
factCards.definition: Radical deputies who moved to Stuttgart were dispersed by Württemberg troops on 18 June 1849.
Prussia's plan for a union of princes without Austria was abandoned at Olmütz in November 1850 under Austrian and Russian pressure.

factCards.term: Why the 1848 revolution failed: four reasons
factCards.definition: The Assembly had no army; the rulers' armies stayed loyal; liberals, radicals and peasants divided; and Frederick William IV refused the crown.
He wrote that German history reached its turning point in 1848 and failed to turn, implying Germany missed its chance of liberal unification.
